claims.text: The as-processed baseline is a predominantly uniform, disordered BCC refractory HEA without significant coherent precipitates.
Aging at approximately 600 °C for approximately 120 hours is an appropriate intervention for the proposed alloy.
The proposed thermal aging will produce a fine dispersion of coherent nanoprecipitates in a BCC matrix.
The aging-induced precipitates will be L1₂ or B2 type.
The targeted precipitates will be smaller than approximately 50 nm.
The precipitates will impede dislocation motion.
The precipitates will remain effective barriers to dislocation motion at temperatures of at least 1000 °C.
The aged alloy will have greater high-temperature yield strength than the as-processed alloy.
The aged alloy will have greater high-temperature creep resistance than the as-processed alloy.
The expected high-temperature improvement applies under steady or cyclic loading at temperatures of at least 1000 °C.
The aging treatment will preserve room-temperature ductility relative to the as-processed alloy.
The aging treatment will preserve room-temperature strength relative to the as-processed alloy.
Coherency of the precipitates will avoid detrimental phase-boundary effects and thereby prevent loss of room-temperature performance.
The treatment and resulting precipitation will not significantly change the alloy's density.
Excessive precipitate coarsening would reduce strengthening or harm room-temperature properties.
A controlled comparison of aged and as-processed specimens, with room-temperature tests, high-temperature tensile and creep tests, and TEM characterization, can test the hypothesis.
Failure to form the targeted precipitates, failure to obtain a statistically significant high-temperature improvement, or degradation of room-temperature properties would falsify the hypothesis.
